stem: A team compares a classic model with hand-crafted features against a deep learning model for classifying product photos. Why does the deep learning model need far more data but no manual feature design?

choices.text: It needs no training data because it is pretrained on rules
It stores every training image and looks them up
It uses fixed if-then rules written by experts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers that learn hierarchical features (edges, shapes, objects) directly from raw data. That removes manual feature engineering but requires large datasets and compute.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rules: that's rule-based systems.
• Lookup: that's memorization, not learning.
• No data: deep models learn from data.

Key takeaway: deep learning = learned features, lots of data.

stem: A vendor says, 'We use XGBoost,' and another says, 'Download our churn model file.' Which statement distinguishes these correctly?

choices.text: Both are datasets used for training
XGBoost is a model; the file is the algorithm
Both are models; algorithm is a synonym

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An algorithm is the learning procedure (such as XGBoost). A model is the artifact produced by running that algorithm on data: learned parameters that make predictions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Synonyms: they're different.
• Reversed: incorrect.
• Datasets: neither is data.

Key takeaway: algorithm + data → model.

stem: A company has finished building a fraud-detection model and deployed it so that it evaluates each new transaction as it occurs, returning an approve/decline decision within milliseconds. Which term describes this phase of the model's life?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Using a deployed model to make predictions on new transactions is inferencing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Labeling: preparing training data.
• Training: building the model.
• Feature engineering: preparing inputs.

Key takeaway: predicting with a trained model → inference.

stem: A hiring-screening model trained on ten years of historical hiring data is later found to systematically rank resumes from one demographic group lower than equally qualified resumes from another group. This phenomenon, where a model produces systematically skewed outcomes for certain groups, is best described as which concept?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
A model that systematically disadvantages a group because it learned from skewed historical decisions shows bias.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Underfitting: poor fit overall.
• Reinforcement learning: a training paradigm.
• Overfitting: memorizing training data.

Key takeaway: historical skew → biased models.

stem: A team trains a classification model that achieves 99% accuracy on the training dataset but only 62% accuracy on a held-out test dataset. What does this gap most likely indicate?

choices.text: The training data must be unlabeled.
The model is overfitting the training data and has poor generalization to new, unseen data.
The model has achieved perfect fairness.
The model is underfitting the data.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Very high training accuracy with much lower accuracy on new data means the model is overfitting and generalizes poorly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Must be unlabeled: no.
• Perfect fairness: unrelated.
• Underfitting: would be poor on training too.

Key takeaway: train high, test low → overfitting.

stem: A company wants one model to summarize reports, translate emails, and answer questions in natural language, without training separate models. What kind of model fits, and why?

choices.text: An LLM, a text foundation model for many tasks
A linear regression model trained on text length
An image classification CNN applied to documents
A rules engine with a dictionary for each task

explanation:
Why this is correct:
LLMs are foundation models trained on massive text corpora. They can perform many language tasks such as summarization, translation, and Q&A through prompting.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Linear regression: predicts numbers from features.
• Rules engine: brittle, one task at a time.
• Image CNN: for images.

Key takeaway: many language tasks, one model → LLM.

stem: How does generative AI (GenAI) most fundamentally differ from traditional discriminative machine learning models?

choices.text: GenAI models never require training data, while traditional ML models always do.
GenAI models can only process numerical, tabular data, while traditional ML models process text and images.
GenAI creates new content like text or images; discriminative models predict labels.
There is no meaningful difference; the terms are synonymous.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Generative AI creates new content such as text, images, or code. Discriminative models classify or predict from inputs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No training data: GenAI needs lots.
• Only tabular data: no.
• Synonymous: no.

Key takeaway: generate vs. discriminate.

stem: A company deploys a system that, given a high-level goal, autonomously breaks the goal into subtasks, decides which tools or APIs to call, executes multi-step actions, and adjusts its plan based on intermediate results with minimal human intervention. Which term best describes this system?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
A system that breaks goals into steps and acts autonomously with tools is agentic AI.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Classification model: predicts labels.
• Batch pipeline: scheduled processing.
• Relational database: storage.

Key takeaway: autonomous multi-step action → agentic AI.

stem: A retailer wants to generate personalized product recommendation scores for its entire customer base once every night, processing millions of records together, with results used the next morning. Latency for any individual prediction is not a concern. Which type of inferencing best fits this requirement?

choices.text: Low-latency asynchronous inferencing with sub-second response requirements
Serverless inferencing invoked per web click

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Scoring the whole customer base periodically, without immediate responses, fits batch inferencing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Sub-second async: unnecessary.
• Real-time: per-request latency not needed.
• Serverless per click: not bulk scoring.

Key takeaway: bulk offline predictions → batch inference.

stem: Which description best characterizes serverless inference for a machine learning model?

choices.text: Capacity is provisioned and scaled automatically; no servers to manage.
The model runs on a dedicated, always-on EC2 instance that the customer must patch and manage.
The model can only make predictions once per day.
Inference requests are stored indefinitely without ever being processed.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Serverless inference automatically provisions and scales compute for requests, and you pay only for usage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dedicated always-on instance: not serverless.
• Once per day: no.
• Requests never processed: no.

Key takeaway: serverless = managed, on-demand capacity.

stem: A company has 50,000 support tickets, each already tagged with a category, and wants to auto-route new tickets. What type of data and learning is this?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tickets with known categories are labeled examples. Training a classifier on labeled examples to predict categories for new tickets is supervised learning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unlabeled/clustering: labels already exist.
• Time-series: not the structure here.
• Reinforcement learning: learns from rewards, not labels.

Key takeaway: known answers in the data → supervised learning.

stem: A finance team needs to calculate exact, deterministic monthly interest accrual for millions of loan accounts using a fixed, well-defined formula, with results that must be 100% precisely reproducible for audit purposes. Which approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Use standard deterministic software; ML adds needless approximation error.
Train a deep learning regression model to approximate the interest calculations.
Use a foundation model to generate the interest figures.
Use unsupervised clustering to group accounts and estimate interest per cluster.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Exact, deterministic calculations like interest accrual should use standard software, not probabilistic AI.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DL approximation: introduces error.
• FM generating figures: unreliable.
• Clustering: irrelevant.

Key takeaway: deterministic rules → traditional software, not AI.

stem: A factory wants cameras to flag scratched products on an assembly line in real time, with minimal ML expertise. Which AI capability and service fit?

choices.text: Time-series forecasting with a regression model
Speech recognition with Amazon Transcribe on line audio
Computer vision, e.g., Rekognition Custom Labels

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Detecting visual defects is a computer vision task. Rekognition Custom Labels can train a defect detector from a modest number of labeled images without deep ML expertise.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Comprehend: text.
• Transcribe: speech.
• Forecasting: predicts future values, not image defects.

Key takeaway: images → computer vision.

stem: A company receives 20,000 emails a day in several languages and wants each tagged by sentiment and key phrases, with no ML team. Which service fits?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Comprehend is a managed NLP service that detects sentiment, key phrases, entities, and language in text, with no model training needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rekognition: images and video.
• Polly: text to speech.
• Textract: extracts text from documents.

Key takeaway: text analytics → Comprehend.

stem: A media company needs to convert recorded customer service phone calls into written text transcripts for analysis, and separately needs to convert written text scripts into natural-sounding spoken audio for an IVR system. Which pair of AWS services matches these two needs, respectively?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transcribe converts call recordings to text, and Polly converts scripts to speech, in that order.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lex and Rekognition: chatbots and images.
• Translate and Comprehend: languages and text analysis.
• Polly then Transcribe: reversed order.

Key takeaway: speech→text = Transcribe; text→speech = Polly.

stem: A streaming service wants each user's home page to show titles based on their history and similar users' behavior, updated as they watch. Which AI use case is this?

choices.text: Anomaly detection on each user's viewing history

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Recommendation systems predict items a user will like from behavior and similar users. Amazon Personalize provides managed, real-time recommendations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Anomaly detection: unusual patterns.
• Text extraction: documents.
• Speech synthesis: audio output.

Key takeaway: personalized suggestions → recommendation systems.

stem: A credit card company wants to flag transactions that deviate significantly from a cardholder's normal spending patterns in real time as potentially fraudulent. Which combination of ML characteristics is most relevant to this use case?

choices.text: A batch inference job that scores all transactions once per month.
A text-generation foundation model used to write summaries of past fraud cases.
An unsupervised clustering model with no labeled fraud examples used at all, evaluated only offline.
Classification or anomaly-detection models scored in real time.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Classification or anomaly-detection models trained on historical transaction patterns flag unusual transactions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Once-a-day batch: too slow for fraud.
• Text generation: wrong task.
• Clustering without labels only: less precise when labels exist.

Key takeaway: fraud detection → classification/anomaly detection.

stem: A retailer must predict next quarter's weekly sales per store, including seasonality and holidays, with a range of likely values. Which technique fits?

choices.text: Clustering of store locations by past sales volume

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Forecasting uses historical values over time plus related factors (holidays, promotions) to predict future values, often with intervals to express uncertainty.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Classification: predicts categories.
• Clustering: groups items.
• Sentiment: text opinion.

Key takeaway: future numbers over time → forecasting.

stem: A company wants employees to ask natural-language questions and receive answers grounded in the company's internal documents, with the system retrieving relevant document excerpts before generating a response so that answers stay accurate and up to date. Which approach does this describe?

choices.text: Training an entirely new foundation model from scratch on the company's documents.
A purely rules-based keyword search engine with no generative component.
Reinforcement learning from scratch with no foundation model involved.
RAG using a knowledge base of the company's documents.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RAG with a knowledge base retrieves relevant company documents and grounds the model's answers in them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Train new FM: costly.
• Keyword search only: no generated answers.
• RL from scratch: unsuitable.

Key takeaway: answers from company documents → RAG.

stem: A company wants to build a conversational chatbot that customers can talk to using voice or text to complete tasks like checking an order status. Separately, the company wants to extract key phrases and entities from stored customer feedback text. Which AWS services should the company use for the chatbot and the text-analysis task, respectively?

choices.text: Amazon Translate for the chatbot, Amazon Transcribe for the text analysis
Amazon Lex for the chatbot, Amazon Comprehend for the text analysis
Amazon Comprehend for the chatbot, Amazon Lex for the text analysis

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon Lex builds voice and text chatbots, and Amazon Comprehend extracts key phrases and entities from text.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Translate and Transcribe: languages and speech-to-text.
• Polly for both: text to speech only.
• Swapped: incorrect.

Key takeaway: chatbot → Lex; text analysis → Comprehend.

stem: A company needs to classify support tickets into one of five fixed, well-understood categories using a modest, well-labeled historical dataset, and wants to minimize ongoing inference cost per prediction. Which approach is the better tradeoff compared to using a large general-purpose foundation model?

choices.text: Use reinforcement learning with no historical data at all.
Always use the largest available foundation model regardless of the task, because bigger models are always cheaper to run.
Use unsupervised clustering instead of the five known categories.
Train a smaller, purpose-built ML classifier on the labeled data.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Five fixed, well-understood categories fit a smaller, purpose-built classifier trained on labeled tickets, which is cheaper and efficient.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RL without data: no.
• Largest FM always: wasteful.
• Clustering: ignores known labels.

Key takeaway: simple classification → traditional ML.

stem: A team deployed a model straight after training and it failed in production due to untested edge cases and changing data. Which pipeline order would have prevented this?

choices.text: Collect, prepare, train, evaluate, deploy, monitor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The ML lifecycle collects and prepares data, trains, evaluates before release, deploys, and then monitors to catch drift and trigger retraining.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Other orders: skip evaluation before deployment or put steps before their inputs exist.

Key takeaway: evaluate before deploy; monitor after.

stem: A dataset has missing values, duplicate rows, and inconsistent date formats. The team also creates a 'days since last purchase' column. Which stage is this?

choices.text: Model monitoring after deployment to production

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cleaning data and creating new features happen during data preparation and feature engineering, before training.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deployment and monitoring: after training.
• Problem framing: before data work.

Key takeaway: clean and shape data before training.

stem: A company is deciding how to serve a foundation model in production. One option is to call a fully managed model API where AWS handles the underlying infrastructure, scaling, and patching. The other option is to self-host the model on customer-managed compute infrastructure for maximum control over the environment. What is a key tradeoff of choosing the self-hosted option over the managed API?

choices.text: Self-hosting eliminates all operational responsibility for the company.
Managed APIs always cost more than self-hosting in every scenario.
Self-hosting is always faster to set up than calling a managed API.
Self-hosting adds control but also operational burden.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Self-hosting gives more control over infrastructure and customization but increases operational responsibility compared with a managed API.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Eliminates operations: opposite.
• Managed always costs more: not always.
• Self-hosting faster: usually slower.

Key takeaway: control vs. operational burden.

stem: A software development team wants an AI assistant embedded in their IDE that can autonomously plan and implement multi-step coding tasks from a written specification, while also considering a separate generative AI assistant that answers questions and automates tasks across various work activities like code review, troubleshooting, and general Q&A. Which two offerings match the IDE-based spec-driven coding assistant and the broader assistant, respectively?

choices.text: Kiro and Amazon Q are the exact same product under two different names
Amazon Q for the spec-driven coding IDE assistant, and Kiro for the broader assistant
Kiro for spec-driven coding; Amazon Q for broader tasks
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart for both needs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Kiro is the spec-driven IDE coding assistant. Amazon Q is the broader assistant across tasks such as code review and troubleshooting.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same product: no.
• Swapped: incorrect.
• JumpStart: model hub.

Key takeaway: spec-driven coding → Kiro; broad assistant → Amazon Q.

stem: Two data scientists retrain the same model a month apart and get different results, and nobody knows which code, data, or settings were used. Which MLOps principle is missing?

choices.text: Lower inference latency for the deployed endpoint
Repeatability via versioned code, data, and settings
A higher number of training epochs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Repeatability means runs can be reproduced because code, data, and configuration are versioned and pipelines are automated (for example, with SageMaker Pipelines).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scalability, latency, epochs: unrelated to reproducing results.

Key takeaway: version everything to reproduce results.

stem: Over time, a team's ML system has accumulated numerous undocumented data dependencies, manually patched pipeline scripts, and glue code that no one fully understands, making changes increasingly risky and slow. This accumulation of hidden costs and complexity is best described as which concept?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Undocumented dependencies and manual steps accumulating over time are ML technical debt.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data augmentation: more data.
• Real-time inferencing: serving.
• Overfitting: model behavior.

Key takeaway: hidden maintenance burden → technical debt.

stem: A medical screening model is evaluated on a highly imbalanced dataset where only 2% of cases are actually positive for a disease. The model achieves 98% overall accuracy simply by predicting 'negative' for almost every case, missing most true positive cases. Which metric would best reveal this model's poor ability to correctly identify actual positive cases?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
With only 2% positive cases, recall shows how many actual positives the model catches, which matters for screening.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Training time: not a quality metric.
• Accuracy: misleading with imbalance.
• Cost per user: business metric.

Key takeaway: rare but critical positives → recall.

stem: An ML team expects to go from 5 to 200 models and from thousands to millions of predictions per day. Which MLOps quality must the platform provide?

choices.text: Interpretability of a single model's predictions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Scalability means the platform handles more models and higher volumes, for example through automated pipelines, managed endpoints, and auto scaling, without proportional manual effort.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Repeatability: reproducing runs.
• Interpretability: explaining predictions.
• Manual approval per prediction: doesn't scale.

Key takeaway: growth in models and traffic → scalability.

stem: After deploying a model to a SageMaker AI endpoint, a team wants to continuously track incoming data for statistical drift compared to the training data distribution and receive alerts if drift exceeds a threshold. Which capability supports this need within the ML lifecycle's monitoring stage?

choices.text: AWS Glue DataBrew, which is used only for one-time data preparation before training
SageMaker Model Monitor for data quality and drift
AWS Budgets, which tracks only billing costs
Amazon Polly, which converts text to speech

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Model Monitor tracks incoming data quality and model quality drift on endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DataBrew: one-time preparation.
• Budgets: costs.
• Polly: speech.

Key takeaway: production model monitoring → Model Monitor.

stem: A team's chatbot bill doubled after it began pasting full policy manuals into every prompt, and long replies are sometimes cut off mid-sentence. Which concept explains both effects?

choices.text: Parameters: larger models charge per parameter used
Tokens: billing and limits count input and output tokens
Embeddings: each prompt is billed by vector size
Epochs: each request retrains the model on the prompt before replying

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Models process text as tokens (words or word pieces). Pricing is per input and output token, and context windows and max output settings are counted in tokens, so long prompts raise cost and output limits truncate replies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parameters: model size affects price per token but isn't billed per request.
• Embeddings: separate models and billing.
• Epochs: training concept; inference doesn't retrain.

Key takeaway: cost, context limits, and truncation are all about tokens.

stem: A RAG app answers poorly because each 80-page PDF is embedded as one vector. What should be done before embedding?

choices.text: Raise the temperature to add more detail
Fine-tune the LLM on each PDF
Tokenize each PDF into one very long vector
Chunk the documents into smaller passages

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Chunking splits documents into passages sized for retrieval, so the search returns the specific relevant section instead of a whole document's diluted vector.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One long vector: the same problem.
• Fine-tuning: costly and not needed for retrieval.
• Temperature: randomness, not retrieval.

Key takeaway: good RAG starts with good chunking.

stem: A search for 'cheap flights' should also find documents saying 'low-cost airfare'. What makes this possible?

choices.text: Exact keyword matching on the word cheap

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Embeddings convert text into numeric vectors that capture meaning, so semantically similar phrases are near each other and vector search finds them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keyword match: misses synonyms.
• Sorting: unrelated.
• Temperature: generation randomness.

Key takeaway: meaning-based search → embeddings.

stem: A developer wants to improve the accuracy of an LLM's responses to a specific task without changing the model's weights or providing additional training data. Which technique should the developer use?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Prompt engineering improves responses by refining instructions and examples without changing model weights.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fine-tuning: changes weights.
• Distillation: new smaller model.
• Retraining: heavy.

Key takeaway: improve without training → prompt engineering.

stem: Older models processed text word by word and struggled with long-range references. Which innovation lets modern LLMs process sequences in parallel and relate distant words?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Self-attention lets each token weigh every other token in the sequence at once, enabling parallel processing and long-range context.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Decision trees, k-means, lookup tables: not the basis of modern LLMs.

Key takeaway: LLMs are built on transformers.

stem: How does a foundation model differ from a traditional, task-specific machine learning model?

choices.text: A foundation model never requires any labeled data during its lifecycle
A foundation model is pretrained broadly and adaptable to many tasks
A foundation model can only ever be used for the single task it was originally trained on
A foundation model always runs faster than a traditional model at inference time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A foundation model is pretrained on broad, diverse data and adapted to many tasks. Traditional models are trained for one task.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Never needs labeled data: may need it for fine-tuning.
• Single task only: opposite.
• Always faster: no.

Key takeaway: FMs are general-purpose and adaptable.

stem: An insurer wants customers to upload a photo of car damage and ask 'How bad is this?' and receive a text answer, using one model. Which model type fits?

choices.text: A speech-to-text model with an image caption step
A multimodal model (image + text in, text out)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multimodal models accept multiple input types, such as images and text, and generate responses that reason over both.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Text-only: can't see the photo.
• Speech-to-text: audio.
• Forecasting: numbers over time.

Key takeaway: mixed inputs → multimodal.

stem: Which description best matches how a diffusion model generates a new image?

choices.text: It translates the text prompt word by word into pixel values using a lookup table
It applies convolution filters to an existing input image to sharpen its edges
It iteratively denoises random noise, guided by the prompt
It retrieves the closest matching image from a fixed database of stored images

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A diffusion model starts from random noise and iteratively denoises it into an image guided by the prompt.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Word-by-word pixel mapping: no.
• Convolution on existing image: no.
• Retrieval: no.

Key takeaway: diffusion = iterative denoising.

stem: In the development of a generative AI application, what does context engineering primarily refer to?

choices.text: Setting only the temperature and top-p sampling parameters for a model
Writing the low-level code that trains a transformer model from random initialization
Selecting and structuring the context given to the model
Configuring the physical network infrastructure that hosts the model

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Context engineering selects and structures the information given to the model, such as retrieved documents, instructions, and history.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only sampling parameters: no.
• Training code: no.
• Network infrastructure: no.

Key takeaway: context engineering = what the model sees.

stem: A generative AI system uses an orchestrator agent that breaks a complex user request into subtasks and delegates each subtask to a specialized agent, for example one agent for web search and another for code execution. What is this pattern called?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
An orchestrator agent splitting work among specialized agents is multi-agent orchestration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fine-tuning: training.
• Distillation: compression.
• RAG: retrieval.

Key takeaway: coordinated agents → multi-agent orchestration.

stem: What is the primary purpose of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) in agentic AI systems?

choices.text: To standardize how agents connect to tools and data
To automatically fine-tune a foundation model on new data
To compress foundation model weights for faster inference
To encrypt all data transmitted between a user and a foundation model

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MCP standardizes how AI agents discover and connect to tools and data sources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fine-tuning: no.
• Compression: no.
• Encryption: no.

Key takeaway: tool connectivity standard → MCP.

stem: A company uses one foundation model for summaries, emails, classification, and Q&A just by changing prompts. Which generative AI advantage is this?

choices.text: No need for any data governance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Foundation models adapt to many tasks through prompting or light customization, instead of one model per task.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deterministic: outputs vary.
• Guaranteed accuracy: hallucinations happen.
• No governance: still needed.

Key takeaway: one model, many tasks → adaptability.

stem: A support chatbot states a 90-day return window, but company policy is 30 days, and the answer sounds confident. Which risk is this, and which mitigation fits BEST?

choices.text: Hallucination; ground answers in policy documents (RAG)
Latency; enable streaming so correct answers arrive sooner for users
Overfitting; use a smaller model with fewer parameters
Data drift; retrain the model weekly on chat logs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Hallucination is fluent but unsupported output. Retrieval-augmented generation supplies the actual policy text, and grounding checks can flag answers not supported by it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data drift: a change in input data over time.
• Overfitting: a training issue, not this behavior.
• Latency: speed, not correctness.

Key takeaway: confident but wrong → ground the model in trusted sources.

stem: A GenAI assistant cut support handling time by 30%, saving $400K a year, and cost $150K to build and run. Which metric expresses this?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
ROI compares the benefit ($400K) with the cost ($150K), expressing business value.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Accuracy: model quality.
• Tokens per second: speed.
• MTBF: reliability.

Key takeaway: business value → ROI.

stem: An e-commerce company adds a generative AI shopping assistant to its website and wants to measure the percentage of site visitors who complete a purchase after interacting with the assistant, compared to before it was added. Which metric should the company track?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Conversion rate shows whether the shopping assistant turns visits into purchases, measuring business impact.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency, F1, token throughput: technical metrics.

Key takeaway: business value → business KPIs.

stem: A subscription streaming service uses generative AI to create personalized content recommendations and wants to know whether this feature increases the average amount of revenue generated per subscriber. Which metric directly measures this?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Average revenue per user shows whether personalized recommendations increase revenue per subscriber.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hallucination rate, precision, accuracy: model metrics.

Key takeaway: revenue impact → ARPU.

stem: A retail company wants to evaluate whether a generative AI-powered loyalty chatbot increases the total projected revenue a typical customer will generate over their entire relationship with the company, not just in a single transaction. Which metric is most appropriate for this evaluation?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Customer lifetime value captures whether the loyalty chatbot increases long-term customer value.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Token limit, inference cost: technical.
• Single transaction: short-term.

Key takeaway: loyalty impact → CLV.

stem: A startup wants to try models from several providers through one API, with no servers or GPUs to manage, and keep its data out of model training. Which service fits?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock is a serverless service providing API access to foundation models from Amazon and third parties. Customer prompts and outputs aren't used to train the base models.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EC2 GPUs: you manage infrastructure and models.
• Ground Truth: labeling.
• Comprehend: fixed NLP tasks.

Key takeaway: many FMs, one serverless API → Bedrock.

stem: A data science team wants to quickly deploy a pre-built, open-source foundation model to a hosted endpoint and optionally fine-tune it on their own dataset, using a curated model hub within their existing Amazon SageMaker AI environment. Which capability should they use?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker JumpStart offers pre-built open-source foundation models that can be deployed to endpoints quickly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: best practices.
• Kiro: IDE assistant.
• Q Business: enterprise assistant.

Key takeaway: deploy open models quickly → JumpStart.

stem: A company wants employees to ask questions across SharePoint, Confluence, and S3 documents, with answers citing sources and respecting each user's existing document permissions, without building an application. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Bedrock with a custom-built application
Amazon Kendra alone with a search page

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Q Business is a managed generative AI assistant that connects to enterprise sources through connectors, cites sources, and enforces users' document access permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bedrock app: possible but requires building the application.
• Kendra alone: search, not a full assistant.
• Comprehend: text analytics.

Key takeaway: ready-made enterprise assistant → Q Business.

stem: A developer wants to build an AI agent using a lightweight, code-first, open-source SDK that lets them define the agent's behavior primarily by writing a system prompt and a list of tools, rather than building an extensive orchestration graph by hand. Which offering fits this description?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Strands Agents SDK is a lightweight, code-first, open-source SDK for building AI agents.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue: ETL.
• Step Functions: workflows.
• EventBridge: events.

Key takeaway: code-first agents → Strands Agents.

stem: A company has built AI agents using several different frameworks and now needs a way to securely deploy, run, and scale these agents in production with enterprise-grade session isolation and identity management, regardless of which framework built them. Which AWS capability is designed for this purpose?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore securely deploys and operates agents built with various frameworks, with runtime, identity, and observability services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Knowledge Bases: RAG.
• Identity Center: workforce access.
• Guardrails: safety filters.

Key takeaway: operate agents at scale → AgentCore.

stem: A startup with a small team and no dedicated ML infrastructure staff wants to add generative AI features to its product quickly. Compared to training a foundation model from scratch on self-managed infrastructure, what is a key advantage of using a managed AWS generative AI service such as Amazon Bedrock?

choices.text: It removes the need to manage ML infrastructure
It eliminates all ongoing usage costs entirely
It guarantees the resulting application will have zero hallucinations
It requires the startup to use only a single, fixed foundation model with no ability to switch

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock lowers the barrier to entry by removing the need to manage ML infrastructure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No usage costs: false.
• Zero hallucinations: false.
• Single fixed model: many models available.

Key takeaway: managed FMs reduce infrastructure burden.

stem: A board member asks whether using Amazon Bedrock means AWS is responsible for everything about the chatbot's security. Which answer is correct?

choices.text: The company must patch the model servers and data centers
AWS is responsible for all security, including user access
AWS secures infrastructure; you secure data and access
Security is shared only for data stored in S3

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Under shared responsibility, AWS secures the infrastructure and the managed service. The customer configures access (IAM), protects its data, sets guardrails, and governs how the application is used.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS responsible for all: customers own access and data decisions.
• Customer patching servers: AWS handles the infrastructure.
• S3 only: applies across services.

Key takeaway: managed doesn't mean hands-off.

stem: A company is deciding whether to use an off-the-shelf foundation model through Amazon Bedrock or invest in customizing and hosting its own fine-tuned custom model. What is a key tradeoff of choosing the custom model approach?

choices.text: Custom models always have lower operational cost than using a managed, shared foundation model
Custom models eliminate the need for any evaluation before production use
Custom models fit better but cost more time and expertise
Custom models are automatically available across all AWS Regions with no additional configuration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Custom models can be tailored to the company's domain, at more cost and effort than off-the-shelf models.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Always lower cost: no.
• No evaluation needed: no.
• Automatically available everywhere: no.

Key takeaway: customization trades effort for fit.

stem: Users in a specific geographic region report higher latency when calling a foundation model hosted through Amazon Bedrock in a distant AWS Region. What is the most direct way this latency issue relates to AWS GenAI infrastructure cost and performance tradeoffs?

choices.text: Provisioned throughput automatically relocates to the nearest Region with no additional configuration
Latency is unrelated to AWS Region selection and depends only on which foundation model is chosen
Using a Region closer to users reduces network latency
Latency can only be fixed by switching to a completely different cloud provider

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Using or replicating the workload in a Region closer to users reduces network latency (or use cross-Region inference options).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Provisioned throughput relocates: no.
• Latency unrelated to Region: false.
• Must change providers: no.

Key takeaway: latency depends on distance.

stem: A chatbot will handle 5 million requests a month with short answers, where a mid-size model already meets quality goals. Which factor should MOST drive the choice between that model and a larger one?

choices.text: The larger model's higher benchmark ranking
Cost per request at this volume

explanation:
Why this is correct:
When quality requirements are met, cost at scale (tokens × volume) and latency usually decide. Bigger models cost more per token.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Popularity, branding, parameter count: not requirements.

Key takeaway: meet the quality bar at the lowest cost.

stem: A financial trading firm needs an FM-powered assistant that returns responses well under 200 milliseconds to support real-time decisions, even if it means using a smaller or less capable model. Which FM characteristic is the firm prioritizing, and what is it trading off?

choices.text: Context window size, trading off latency
Latency, trading off some response quality/capability for speed

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Strict response-time needs prioritize latency, often trading some capability for a faster model.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Context window, multilingual, modality: not the main constraint.

Key takeaway: latency-critical → faster, smaller models.

stem: A support center serves customers in Korean, Spanish, and English and wants one foundation model. Which selection criterion matters MOST?

choices.text: The size of its training dataset only
Support for video input and long video summaries
Multilingual capability in the needed languages

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The model must understand and respond well in all the required languages. Test it on real samples in each language.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Images or video: not needed.
• Training data size alone: doesn't guarantee language quality.

Key takeaway: choose models by the task's requirements.

stem: A company currently uses a very large, general-purpose FM to classify short product reviews as positive or negative. Inference is slow and expensive for this simple task. Which change would MOST directly reduce cost and latency while likely maintaining acceptable accuracy for this narrow task?

choices.text: Increase the maximum output token limit
Switch to a smaller, less complex model appropriately sized for the task
Add more few-shot examples to every prompt

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A smaller model sized for simple review classification cuts cost and latency with adequate accuracy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Higher output limit: more cost.
• Higher temperature: less consistency.
• More examples: more tokens.

Key takeaway: right-size the model to the task.

stem: An application repeatedly sends the same long system instructions and reference document as part of every prompt to an FM on Amazon Bedrock, with only the user's question changing each time. Which feature can reduce cost and latency by reusing the processed state of the repeated portion of the prompt?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Prompt caching stores repeated prompt prefixes (such as long instructions and documents), reducing cost and latency on reuse.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Knowledge Bases: retrieval.
• Distillation: training.
• Fine-tuning: training.

Key takeaway: repeated prompt content → prompt caching.

stem: A legal drafting assistant produces different clause wording each time, which reviewers dislike. A marketing tool should produce varied slogans. Which setting should be adjusted, and how?

choices.text: Model size: smaller for legal, larger for marketing
Context window: shorter for legal, longer for marketing
Temperature: lower for legal, higher for marketing
Max tokens: lower for legal, higher for marketing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Temperature controls randomness. Low values give more consistent output, and higher values give more variety.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Max tokens: length, not variety.
• Context window: how much input fits.
• Model size: capability, not variety.

Key takeaway: consistency vs. creativity → temperature.

stem: A developer sets an FM's maximum output token limit very low to reduce cost. Users now report that generated answers are frequently cut off mid-sentence for complex questions. What is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: The model does not support the requested input modality
The temperature parameter is set too high
The max output length parameter is too low

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A very low maximum output token limit cuts responses off mid-answer.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Modality: unrelated.
• High temperature: affects randomness.
• Prompt caching: unrelated.

Key takeaway: truncated answers → max output tokens.

stem: An HR chatbot gives outdated leave policies because the policy changed after the model was trained. Which technique fixes this without retraining?

choices.text: Increase the temperature so the model explores newer policies
Pre-train a new model from scratch
RAG: retrieve current policies into the prompt

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Retrieval-augmented generation fetches relevant, current documents at request time and adds them to the prompt, so answers reflect the latest information.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pre-training: very costly and still becomes outdated.
• Temperature: randomness only.
• Removing the system prompt: less control.

Key takeaway: current knowledge → retrieval, not retraining.

stem: A company wants its FM-powered assistant to answer questions using internal product documentation that changes frequently, without retraining the model every time the documentation is updated. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Fine-tune the FM every time documentation changes
Implement RAG using Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock
Continuously pretrain the FM on the documentation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RAG with Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock retrieves current internal documentation at query time, grounding answers without retraining.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fine-tune on every change: slow and costly.
• Continuous pretraining: heavy.
• Higher temperature: more random.

Key takeaway: answer from changing documents → RAG.

stem: Which of the following AWS services can be used to store and query vector embeddings for a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) solution? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL (using the pgvector extension)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector and OpenSearch Service can both store and query vector embeddings for RAG.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Step Functions, SNS, Glue: not vector stores.

Key takeaway: vector stores → pgvector, OpenSearch (and others).

stem: A company is comparing ways to customize an FM for its use case. Ordering the following approaches from LOWEST to HIGHEST typical cost and implementation complexity, which sequence is correct?

choices.text: Fine-tuning < Prompt engineering < RAG < Full pretraining
Prompt engineering (in-context learning) < RAG < Fine-tuning < Full pretraining
RAG < Full pretraining < Prompt engineering < Fine-tuning
Full pretraining < Fine-tuning < RAG < Prompt engineering

explanation:
Why this is correct:
From least to most effort and cost: prompt engineering, then RAG, then fine-tuning, then full pretraining.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Other orders: misrank effort.

Key takeaway: customization effort increases in this order.

stem: A prompt says 'Draft a reply to this customer,' and the output ignores the customer's order history. What should be added to the prompt?

choices.text: A random seed value so the reply stays consistent
Context: the relevant order history and details

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Context is the background information the model needs, such as the customer's history, so it can produce a relevant response.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Max tokens: length only.
• Seed: repeatability.
• Shorter instruction: removes guidance.

Key takeaway: the model only knows what you give it.

stem: A prompt includes an article and some examples but the model returns a list of keywords instead of a summary. Which prompt element is missing or unclear?

choices.text: The model version number and provider name

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The instruction tells the model what to do, for example 'Summarize this article in 3 sentences.' Without a clear instruction, the model guesses the task.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Temperature, version, price: not prompt elements that define the task.

Key takeaway: say explicitly what task you want.

stem: A team uses an FM to generate marketing images and wants to prevent the model from including any text or watermarks in the generated images. Which prompt engineering technique should they use?

choices.text: A negative prompt specifying elements to exclude

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A negative prompt lists elements to exclude from generated images.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Few-shot: examples.
• Chain-of-thought: reasoning.
• Higher temperature: more randomness.

Key takeaway: exclude elements → negative prompts.

stem: A developer wants an FM to solve multi-step math word problems more accurately by having it explicitly work through intermediate reasoning steps before giving a final answer. Which prompting technique should the developer use?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to reason step by step, improving multi-step math accuracy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Negative prompting: exclusions.
• Templating: consistency.
• Zero-shot: no reasoning guidance.

Key takeaway: multi-step reasoning → chain of thought.

stem: A zero-shot sentiment prompt mislabels sarcastic reviews. Which change is the simplest improvement, and what is it called?

choices.text: Fine-tune the model on millions of reviews

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Zero-shot gives no examples. Few-shot prompting adds a handful of labeled examples, including tricky ones such as sarcasm, which often improves accuracy quickly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fine-tuning: heavier than needed first.
• No instructions: worse.
• Image model: wrong modality.

Key takeaway: zero-shot → few-shot before customization.

stem: A prompt includes exactly one example pairing an input with its desired output before asking the model to complete a new, similar task. Which technique is this?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Exactly one example before the task is single-shot (one-shot) prompting.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Zero-shot: no examples.
• Few-shot: several examples.
• Chain-of-thought: reasoning steps.

Key takeaway: one example → one-shot.

stem: A company has hundreds of employees writing prompts for internal FM-powered tools and wants consistent structure, tone, and required fields such as role, context, and task across all prompts. Which practice would BEST support this goal?

choices.text: Increasing the temperature for every prompt

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Standardized prompt templates give many employees consistent, tested prompts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Higher temperature: less consistency.
• Disable guardrails: unsafe.
• Zero-shot only: less guidance.

Key takeaway: consistency at scale → templates.

stem: A team's prompts frequently produce inconsistent or overly broad responses from an FM. Which best practice is MOST likely to improve response quality?

choices.text: Avoiding the use of any examples in the prompt
Making prompts more specific and iteratively experimenting with wording
Maximizing the temperature parameter for every request
Removing all task instructions from the prompt

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Making prompts more specific and iterating on wording reduces inconsistent or overly broad responses.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Avoid examples: less guidance.
• Max temperature: more variation.
• Remove instructions: worse.

Key takeaway: specific prompts → focused answers.

stem: Which term describes crafting prompts specifically designed to bypass an FM's built-in safety and content moderation restrictions so it produces normally disallowed content?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Crafting prompts to bypass a model's safety controls is jailbreaking.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Distillation, chain-of-thought, fine-tuning: other concepts.

Key takeaway: bypassing safety → jailbreaking.

stem: A malicious actor deliberately inserts corrupted or biased examples into a dataset that will later be used to fine-tune an FM, intending to manipulate the model's future behavior. This risk is known as:
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deliberately inserting corrupted or biased examples into training data is data (prompt) poisoning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Prompt hijacking: manipulating runtime prompts.
• Zero-shot leakage: not a term here.
• Model exposure: not this.

Key takeaway: tainted training data → poisoning.

stem: A company wants to create, test, save multiple versions of, and track which version of a prompt is deployed to production across several applications. Which Amazon Bedrock feature is designed for this purpose?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Prompt Management for Amazon Bedrock creates, tests, versions, and tracks prompts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Model Evaluation: compares models.
• Guardrails: safety.
• Knowledge Bases: RAG.

Key takeaway: prompt versioning → Prompt Management.

stem: A startup is considering building its own foundation model from scratch. What does this pretraining step involve?

choices.text: Training on massive data with huge compute
Fine-tuning an existing model on 1,000 records
Adding a few examples to a prompt

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pretraining trains a model from scratch on very large, broad datasets to learn general patterns. It requires enormous compute and cost, so most companies start from existing foundation models.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Few-shot prompts, fine-tuning, and retrieval: all build on an existing pretrained model.

Key takeaway: pretraining is rarely the right starting point for a business.

stem: A law firm wants a model to write in its specific clause style consistently. It has 5,000 labeled examples of prompts and ideal outputs. Which customization fits?

choices.text: Pretraining a new model from scratch

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fine-tuning further trains a pretrained model on task-specific labeled examples, teaching consistent style and format.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pretraining: unnecessary and costly.
• Temperature: randomness.
• Guardrails: restrict content; they don't teach style.

Key takeaway: consistent task-specific behavior from labeled examples → fine-tuning.

stem: A company wants to keep its FM current with an ongoing stream of new, unlabeled domain-specific text, using the same self-supervised training objective as the model's original training, without creating labeled examples. Which approach is this?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Continuous pretraining uses ongoing unlabeled domain data to keep a model's knowledge current.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RLHF: human feedback alignment.
• Templating: prompts.
• Instruction fine-tuning: labeled pairs.

Key takeaway: unlabeled domain updates → continuous pretraining.

stem: A company trains a smaller 'student' model to replicate the behavior and outputs of a larger, more capable 'teacher' FM, aiming to reduce inference cost and latency while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Which technique is this?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Training a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher is model distillation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Continuous pretraining, RAG, domain adaptation: other techniques.

Key takeaway: smaller copy of a big model → distillation.

stem: A company fine-tunes an FM using a dataset of paired instructions and desired responses, such as 'Write a summary' paired with an example summary, so the model becomes better at following natural-language commands. Which fine-tuning method is this?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fine-tuning on paired instructions and desired responses is instruction tuning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Continuous pretraining: unlabeled.
• Domain adaptation: domain corpus.
• Transfer learning: broad concept.

Key takeaway: instruction-response pairs → instruction tuning.

stem: A general-purpose FM is fine-tuned using a large corpus of legal contracts and case law so it better understands legal terminology and context. This is an example of:
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fine-tuning on legal contracts and case law specializes the model's language and knowledge: domain adaptation fine-tuning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Distillation, RLHF, zero-shot: other methods.

Key takeaway: specialize to a field → domain adaptation.

stem: A team builds a defect detector with only 500 images by starting from a model already trained on millions of general images. What is this approach called?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transfer learning reuses knowledge from a model trained on one task or dataset to improve learning on a related task with less data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reinforcement learning: rewards.
• Clustering: no labels.
• Rules: no learning.

Key takeaway: reuse learned knowledge → transfer learning.

stem: A team fine-tunes an FM on raw customer support transcripts without removing personally identifiable information (PII) or reviewing the data for quality. After deployment, the model occasionally reproduces sensitive customer details in its responses. Which step in the fine-tuning data preparation process was MOST likely neglected?

choices.text: Choosing an evaluation metric such as BLEU
Data curation and governance, including PII removal and quality review

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data curation and governance, including PII removal and consent, should come before fine-tuning on transcripts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• BLEU: evaluation.
• Prompt caching: inference.
• Temperature: inference.

Key takeaway: curate data before training.

stem: A company has only 50 labeled examples for a highly specialized classification task and plans to fine-tune an FM using this dataset. What is the MOST likely risk of fine-tuning with such a small labeled dataset?

choices.text: Reduced ability to run the model on GPU-based infrastructure
Overfitting and poor generalization to new, unseen inputs
Guaranteed improvement over the base FM's performance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With only 50 examples, fine-tuning risks overfitting and poor generalization to new inputs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GPU compatibility: unrelated.
• Guaranteed improvement: no.
• Too-low latency: no.

Key takeaway: tiny datasets → overfitting risk.

stem: A company fine-tunes an FM using training data collected only from customers in one country, then deploys the resulting model globally. Users in other regions report poor and culturally inappropriate responses. Which data preparation principle was MOST likely violated?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data from one country may not represent global users, so representativeness of the training data is the concern.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Labeling consistency: different issue.
• RLHF: not the issue.
• Prompt caching: unrelated.

Key takeaway: training data must represent users.

stem: A model gives correct but rude answers. Reviewers rank pairs of responses, and a reward model trained on those rankings guides further training. What is this technique?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback uses human preference rankings to train a reward model, which then steers the model toward preferred behavior such as helpfulness and tone.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Few-shot: examples in prompts.
• Continued pretraining: more unlabeled domain data.
• Augmentation: expands training data.

Key takeaway: align with human preferences → RLHF.

stem: A company needs its FM responses to reflect information that changes daily, such as current inventory levels, and cannot afford to retrain the model every day. Compared to fine-tuning, which customization approach is MOST cost-effective and appropriate for this requirement?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
RAG retrieves current information at query time without retraining, fitting data that changes daily.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fine-tuning, distillation, pretraining: static knowledge.

Key takeaway: fresh facts → RAG.

stem: Automated scores rate two chatbot versions equally, but customers prefer one. Which evaluation approach captures tone, helpfulness, and brand fit?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Human reviewers judge subjective qualities such as helpfulness, tone, and appropriateness that automatic metrics miss. Bedrock supports human evaluation jobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Token counts, file sizes, GPU use: not quality measures.

Key takeaway: subjective quality → human evaluation.

stem: A team compares three models on its task. Why use a standardized benchmark dataset alongside its own tests?

choices.text: Consistent, repeatable comparison on the same tasks
It guarantees the best benchmark model wins in production
It trains the models to be more accurate
It removes the need for any business testing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Benchmarks give a common, repeatable basis for comparison. They don't replace testing on the company's own data and goals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Guaranteed production win: benchmarks may not reflect your use case.
• No business testing: still needed.
• Training: benchmarks evaluate, they don't train.

Key takeaway: benchmarks compare; your data decides.

stem: A company wants to compare outputs from several FMs available in Amazon Bedrock on the same set of prompts, using either automatic metrics or human evaluators, without building custom evaluation tooling. Which Amazon Bedrock feature should the company use?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model Evaluation in Amazon Bedrock compares multiple models on the same tasks with automatic or human evaluation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Knowledge Bases, Agents, Guardrails: other features.

Key takeaway: compare models → Bedrock Model Evaluation.

stem: Which evaluation metric is commonly used to assess automatically generated text summaries by measuring the overlap of n-grams between the generated summary and one or more human-written reference summaries?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
ROUGE measures overlap between generated summaries and reference summaries, emphasizing recall.

Why the other options are wrong:
• F1: classification.
• BERTScore: embedding similarity.
• BLEU: translation precision.

Key takeaway: summaries → ROUGE.

stem: A team evaluates an FM's machine translation output against human reference translations using a precision-based metric that measures n-gram overlap between the generated translation and the references. Which metric are they MOST likely using?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
BLEU measures n-gram overlap with reference translations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• BERTScore: semantic similarity.
• ROUGE: summaries.
• Perplexity: language modeling.

Key takeaway: translation → BLEU.

stem: Which evaluation metric uses contextual embeddings from a pretrained language model to compute semantic similarity between generated text and reference text, allowing it to capture meaning even when the exact words differ?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
BERTScore uses contextual embeddings to compare semantic similarity between generated and reference text.

Why the other options are wrong:
• BLEU, ROUGE: n-gram overlap.
• Exact match: strict equality.

Key takeaway: semantic similarity → BERTScore.

stem: A company wants to automatically evaluate thousands of long-form FM-generated responses for coherence and helpfulness without hiring human reviewers for every response, while still capturing nuanced judgment beyond simple word overlap. Which evaluation approach BEST fits this need?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
LLM-as-a-judge uses a model to score long responses against criteria at scale.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Poisoning detection: security.
• BLEU only: limited.
• Exact match: unsuitable for long text.

Key takeaway: scalable qualitative evaluation → LLM-as-a-judge.

stem: A company deploys a RAG-based question-answering assistant and wants to evaluate whether the documents retrieved for user queries are actually relevant, in addition to evaluating the final generated answer. Which evaluation focus is unique to RAG applications compared to evaluating a standalone FM?

choices.text: Counting the number of fine-tuning epochs used
Measuring only the model's temperature setting

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RAG evaluation checks retrieval relevance and whether answers are grounded in the retrieved context.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Epochs, latency only, temperature: not answer quality.

Key takeaway: evaluate RAG on retrieval + groundedness.

stem: A company builds an AI agent that plans multiple steps, calls external tools, and completes a multi-step customer request. Which evaluation focus is MOST important and specific to this agentic workflow, beyond evaluating a single FM response?

choices.text: The ROUGE score of only the agent's first response
The storage capacity of the vector database used
Whether the agent completes the whole multi-step task
The temperature parameter used during the model's original pretraining

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Agent evaluation focuses on whether the agent completes the overall multi-step task correctly, including tool use.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ROUGE of first response: incomplete.
• Vector DB size: irrelevant.
• Training temperature: irrelevant.

Key takeaway: agents → task completion.

stem: A chatbot's BLEU and ROUGE scores improved, but leadership asks whether it helps the business. Which metrics answer that?

choices.text: Task completion rate and cost per interaction
Model parameter count and context window size
BLEU score on a new dataset

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Business metrics such as task completion, containment, customer satisfaction, and cost per interaction show whether the application delivers value.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Perplexity, BLEU, parameters: technical measures.

Key takeaway: measure outcomes the business cares about.

stem: An FM-powered support chatbot achieves high BLEU and ROUGE scores against reference answers during testing, but customer satisfaction surveys after launch show low satisfaction. What is the MOST likely explanation?

choices.text: BLEU and ROUGE scores are inversely correlated with model accuracy
The chatbot's temperature parameter was necessarily set to zero
The knowledge base used by the chatbot was not encrypted
N-gram metrics miss real usefulness; add human review

explanation:
Why this is correct:
N-gram overlap metrics don't fully capture relevance, correctness, or helpfulness, so high BLEU and ROUGE can coexist with poor answers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inversely correlated: no.
• Temperature necessarily: no.
• Unencrypted KB: unrelated.

Key takeaway: combine automatic metrics with human judgment.

stem: A medical FAQ bot must give factually correct answers grounded in approved content. Which responsible AI dimension is this?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Veracity and robustness concern producing correct, truthful outputs, supported by grounding and evaluation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Controllability: steering behavior.
• Privacy: protecting data.
• Fairness: equitable outcomes.

Key takeaway: correctness → veracity.

stem: A model answers correctly for clean inputs but fails badly when users add typos or slight rephrasing. Which responsible AI property is lacking?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
Robustness means stable, reliable behavior under variations in input, including noise or small changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transparency and explainability: understanding the model.
• Governance: oversight processes.

Key takeaway: stable under messy inputs → robustness.

stem: A legal team is reviewing risks associated with deploying a generative AI writing assistant. Risk 1: the company is sued for using copyrighted text without authorization. Risk 2: customers lose confidence after the assistant repeatedly invents nonexistent product features. Which option correctly matches Risk 1 and Risk 2, respectively, to their underlying cause?

choices.text: Risk 1 = biased outputs; Risk 2 = intellectual property infringement
Risk 1 = trust loss; Risk 2 = intellectual property infringement
Risk 1 = intellectual property infringement; Risk 2 = hallucination leading to trust loss

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Using copyrighted text is intellectual property infringement (Risk 1). Inventing nonexistent features is hallucination, leading to trust loss (Risk 2).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Other mappings: mismatch the risks.

Key takeaway: IP risk vs. hallucination risk.

stem: A data science team is curating a training dataset for a resume-screening model and wants to reduce the risk of the model unfairly disadvantaging any demographic group. Which dataset practice would best support this goal?

choices.text: Sourcing data only from the company's highest-performing current employees
Removing all demographic-related fields from the dataset after collection with no further review
Using the largest available dataset regardless of its source
Diverse, representative examples from vetted sources

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A diverse, representative dataset reduces bias in resume screening.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Top performers only: skewed.
• Remove demographic fields: proxies remain.
• Largest regardless of source: may be biased.

Key takeaway: fairness starts with representative data.

stem: After deployment, a company discovers its credit-approval model achieves 95% overall accuracy but only 60% accuracy for applicants from a specific demographic subgroup that was underrepresented in training data. Which technique would have best helped the team identify this problem before deployment?

choices.text: Measuring only the overall aggregate accuracy across the entire test set
Increasing the learning rate during training
Subgroup analysis of metrics per demographic segment
Reducing the number of training epochs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Subgroup analysis evaluates performance per demographic group, revealing disparities hidden by overall accuracy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Overall accuracy only: hides gaps.
• Learning rate: unrelated.
• Fewer epochs: unrelated.

Key takeaway: fairness → subgroup metrics.

stem: A model scores 98% in training but 70% on new data, and worst on a small demographic group with few training examples. What is happening?

choices.text: Too much training data for the model's size

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Overfitting means the model memorized training data and generalizes poorly. Groups with few examples suffer most, which also creates fairness issues.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Underfitting: poor on training data too.
• Perfect generalization: contradicted by results.
• Too much data: usually reduces overfitting.

Key takeaway: high train, low test → overfitting; check subgroups.

stem: A responsible AI team wants to (1) check whether human annotators are consistently and correctly assigning labels in a training dataset, and (2) check whether model performance differs meaningfully across demographic segments after deployment. Which two techniques should they use, respectively?

choices.text: Label quality analysis, then subgroup analysis
Subgroup analysis, then label quality analysis
A/B testing, then label quality analysis

explanation:
Why this is correct:
First check label quality (annotator consistency), then run subgroup analysis on model performance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hyperparameter tuning: not fairness analysis.
• Reversed order: labels first.
• A/B testing: not this.

Key takeaway: clean labels before fairness analysis.

stem: A company configures very strict Amazon Bedrock Guardrails content filters to maximize safety. Users soon complain that many legitimate, benign questions are being blocked or heavily redacted. What responsible AI tradeoff does this scenario illustrate?

choices.text: Content filtering strength has no effect on user experience
Guardrails only affect model training, not inference, so this behavior is unrelated to safety configuration
Overly aggressive safety filtering can reduce usability and the system's practical helpfulness
Guardrails automatically resolve this tradeoff without any configuration needed

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Overly strict filters can block legitimate requests, hurting usability. Safety settings must balance protection with user experience.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No effect on UX: false.
• Only training: Guardrails apply at inference.
• Automatically resolved: requires tuning.

Key takeaway: safety vs. usability tradeoff.

stem: A bank's assistant must refuse to give investment advice, even when asked indirectly. Which Bedrock Guardrails feature fits?

choices.text: Denied topics with a definition and examples

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Denied topics describe subjects the application must avoid (with a definition and sample phrases), detecting them even when phrased indirectly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Violence filters: harmful content categories.
• Profanity: specific words.
• Grounding: hallucination checks.

Key takeaway: off-limits subjects → denied topics.

stem: A startup wants to deploy a generative AI feature but has a limited budget and wants to minimize its environmental impact while still meeting business requirements. Which responsible model-selection practice best supports this goal?

choices.text: Evaluate smaller or task-specific models that meet needs
Retrain a new foundation model from scratch for every new use case
Always select the model with the highest parameter count available
Ignore model size and select models solely based on brand recognition

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Evaluating smaller, task-specific or pre-trained models can meet needs at lower cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Retrain FMs each time: costly.
• Largest model: costly.
• Brand-based choice: not cost-aware.

Key takeaway: cost-effective model selection.

stem: Model A shows high bias, consistently underpredicting loan approval rates for one demographic group regardless of individual applicant qualifications. Model B shows high variance, giving wildly inconsistent predictions for similar applicants across groups. Which statement correctly compares the responsible AI implications of these two conditions?

choices.text: Neither condition is relevant to responsible AI because both are purely statistical concepts
Both conditions have identical effects on demographic fairness
High variance always indicates the model is discriminatory, while high bias never affects fairness
Bias disadvantages a group systematically; variance is erratic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
High bias creates a systematic, predictable disadvantage for a group. High variance produces inconsistent, erratic predictions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Irrelevant: no.
• Identical effects: no.
• Variance always discriminatory: no.

Key takeaway: bias = systematic; variance = inconsistent.

stem: A regulator asks how a model works, what data trained it, and its known limits. Which responsible AI concept is this, and which AWS artifact helps?

choices.text: Latency; document it in CloudWatch dashboards
Scalability; document it in Auto Scaling policies
Cost; document it in AWS Budgets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transparency means stakeholders can understand a model's workings, data, and limitations. Model Cards document intended use, training data, evaluation, and risks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scalability, latency, cost: operational topics.

Key takeaway: transparency → documented models.

stem: A company wants to formally document a deployed model's intended use cases, training data sources, performance metrics, and known limitations so that internal reviewers and auditors can evaluate it. Which AWS capability is designed specifically for this purpose?
explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Model Cards document intended use, training data, evaluation results, and limitations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Guardrails: filters.
• CloudTrail: API logs.
• CloudWatch: metrics.

Key takeaway: model documentation → Model Cards.

stem: A company considers publishing the full internal architecture and training data details of its fraud-detection model to increase transparency with regulators. Security reviewers raise concerns that this level of disclosure could help bad actors reverse-engineer ways to evade detection. What responsible AI tradeoff does this scenario best illustrate?

choices.text: Model architecture disclosure has no effect on system security
Regulators never require any transparency about fraud-detection systems
Transparency and safety are always perfectly aligned with no possible conflict
Transparency can conflict with safety and security goals.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Publishing full details of a fraud model could help attackers evade it. Transparency can conflict with safety and security.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No security effect: false.
• Regulators never require transparency: false.
• Always aligned: false.

Key takeaway: transparency must be balanced with security.

stem: A company wants to build a product on an open-source foundation model. Which step best supports responsible and legal use?

choices.text: Skip evaluation because the model is popular
Assume open source means no restrictions
Review the license and model card

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Open models come with licenses that may restrict use cases or require attribution, and documentation describes training data and limits. Both must be reviewed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No restrictions: many licenses have conditions.
• Removing attribution: may violate terms.
• Skipping evaluation: popularity isn't fitness.

Key takeaway: read the license and model card before building.

stem: A company deploying a customer-service chatbot wants to incorporate human-centered design principles for explainability. Which feature would best support this goal?

choices.text: A way for users to flag or rate responses
Removing all user-facing explanations to simplify the interface
Disabling logging of user interactions to reduce storage costs
Restricting chatbot access to internal employees only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Letting users flag or rate responses gives feedback that improves the chatbot and keeps humans in the loop.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove explanations: less transparency.
• Disable logging: no feedback.
• Restrict to employees: avoids users.

Key takeaway: human-centered design → user feedback.

stem: A company already publishes a SageMaker Model Card describing a model's intended use and limitations, but a data scientist argues this is not sufficient for explaining why the model denied a specific customer's application. Which statement best explains the gap?

choices.text: SageMaker Model Cards are only used for tracking billing and cost information
Model cards describe the model, not individual predictions
